ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *bá(r)śtᵊkə, with r-loss before a fricative (see buzë) and postsynocopal simplification of the plosive cluster tᵊk > tk > k, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *bárśtukā-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰórs-tu-kah₂- (“mass of hair”), collective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰorstu-kó- (“hairy”). An origin from Proto-Albanian *baskā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask- (“bundle”), is unlikely as the PIE *-sk- cluster would lead to Albanian -h-, not -shk- (*-sk- > *-hk- > *-kh- > *-kʰ- > -h-). The Proto-Albanian form itself would have been *bakʰā > *bahë.

An origin from Proto-Albanian *baskā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask- (“bundle”), is unlikely as the PIE *-sk- cluster would lead to Albanian -h-, not -shk- (*-sk- > *-hk- > *-kh- > *-kʰ- > -h-). The Proto-Albanian form itself would have been *bakʰā > *bahë.
Borrowed from a South Slavic term derived from the otherwise unattested Proto-Slavic *bolьba, a derivative of *bolь (“pain”).
Either a variant or a derivative of cys.
Unknown. Maybe from Vulgar Latin *ferrusca (“small iron”), from Latin ferrum.
Albanian patronymic surname "descendant of Gjokë". From Gjokë + -aj (“he, descendant of”). See Gjokë for more.

s.g: inedible parts or leftovers of a fruit
the lower social class, the wretched (term used by the upper class)

s.g: to become blue in the face

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *krupa, related to Lithuanian kraupùs (“easily scared”), krupùs, krúpti (“to scare”).

s.g: bride's father or bridegroom's father; male family member of either

ety.text: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin consocer, consocerum. Compare Romanian cuscru.

From Proto-Albanian *lubnaka, from Proto-Indo-European *leubh (“to peel, to skin”). Cognate to Lithuanian lubà (“board (of a ceiling)”), Latvian luba (“bark, board”), Old Prussian lubbo (“board”) and Proto-Slavic *lьbь (“forehead, skull”).

From mbanj (Arbëreshë), from *ënbanj (compare Old Gheg ënbaj), the *m- being from Proto-Albanian *en- (intensive prefix). The identity of the root is disputed. * Orel posits Proto-Albanian *barnja, a causative formed to Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry”). * Schumacher and DPEWA after him insist on a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect”).
Mediopassive form of Albanian nderoj (“to honour”). From nder (“honour(ed)”) + -o + -hem (“to be”).
From perëndoj (“to set”), from the sense dielli (“the sun”) perëndon (“sets”).

s.g: Prizren (the second largest city in Kosovo, and the seat of Prizren District and Prizren Municipality, Kosovo; the historical capital of Kosovo)

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *per-ambi-uptja related to përmbi and ultimately to mbys. The second element *uptja is cognate with Greek ὑπὸ (hupò, “under”), Sanskrit उप (úpa, “towards, near to”) and Gothic uf (“under”).

From Proto-Albanian *rūtja, from Proto-Indo-European *reṷə-. Cognate to Latin ruo (“to rush down, to bring down”), Proto-Slavic *ryti, Lithuanian ráuti (“to tear, to pull”), Egyptian rish (“high leader, boss”).

tpl.gloss: to rush down, to bring down

s.g: place with huts and pens for shepherds and cattle; shed, fold, barn; hut, shelter

ety.text: Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *stanъ (“camp”).
From Proto-Albanian *tangā (“thick forest”), close to Lithuanian tankù, Old Norse þéttr (“thick”). Possibly a derivative of tangë, with a semantic innovation.

s.g: to toast, brown, warm one's feet

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *ϑeuk-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewk- (“to glow, burn, lighten”). Perhaps related to flak (“flame”). Cognates include Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬊𐬐 (saok), Northern Kurdish sotin and Persian سوختن (suxtan, “to burn”). Also compare Ancient Greek τήκω (tḗkō, “melt, dissolve”) Alternatively related to Lithuanian senkù, sèkti (“to sink, to dry up”), Gothic sigqan (“to sink”), Proto-Slavic *sęknǫti (“to dry up”).

s.g: initialism of Teatri Kombëtar i Operas dhe Baletit (“National Theatre of Opera and Ballet of Albania”)

ety.text: From variant zhapik, from Serbo-Croatian žȁbica (“small frog or toad”), diminutive from Proto-Slavic *žaba (“toad, frog”).
From a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ščetina (“bristle”). Compare Serbo-Croatian četina, Macedonian четина (četina).
